subtype: Approach: venting in the group chat [Pitfall]
passage: I'm in the class group chat, so I saw it happen on Sunday night. Rekha posted: "Some people can't keep anything to themselves. Good to know who your real friends are." No names. Within minutes there were twelve replies. "Who??" "Hugs, Rekha." "Is it about you-know-who?" Everyone guessed Trisha, because the two of them had been inseparable until Friday. Trisha didn't reply at all. On Monday she sat at the back, eyes on her desk, and two girls whispered when she walked past. I don't know what Trisha did, or exactly what Rekha was feeling. Rekha looked pleased on Sunday night and miserable by Monday lunch. When Trisha finally walked up to her in the corridor, Rekha turned away. I think the chat had made it too big to talk about.

qa.q: How many replies came within minutes of Rekha's post?
qa.a: Twelve replies.

qa.q: How did Rekha's mood seem to change from Sunday night to Monday?
qa.a: She seemed pleased by the sympathy on Sunday night but miserable by Monday lunch, once the conflict had spread.

qa.q: What could Rekha have done instead of posting?
qa.a: Messaged Trisha privately or asked to talk, so the hurt could be sorted out between the two of them without an audience.

qa.q: What is Monday like for Trisha?
qa.a: Trisha seems embarrassed and isolated, sitting at the back with eyes on the desk while others whisper.

grounding: An observer watches a student's vague post in the class chat draw sympathy, spread the conflict and make a real talk harder.

subtype: Approach: venting in the group chat [Pitfall]
passage:
Friday. Jyoti skips Varun's cricket match to go to the mall with the new kids, after promising to come. Varun waits by the boundary, checking the gate every over.
Saturday. At midnight Varun types into the class group: "Funny how some people only show up when it suits them." Hearts and "bro who??" pour in. For an hour he feels better. Then Jyoti's cousin replies, "If this is about Jyoti, just say it." Screenshots start going round.
Monday. Jyoti won't look at him in the corridor. At lunch, when Varun finally says, "Can we talk?", Jyoti says, "Why? You already told everyone," and walks off. Varun realises he never actually told Jyoti what hurt.

qa.q: What did Varun type into the class group?
qa.a: Funny how some people only show up when it suits them.

qa.q: How did Varun feel after posting?

qa.q: What could Varun do now?

qa.q: Why might Jyoti refuse to talk on Monday?

grounding: Shows over three days how venting in a group chat brings brief sympathy, then spreads the conflict and blocks an honest talk.

subtype: Approach: silent treatment and avoidance [Pitfall]
passage: Abhinav had laughed when the teacher read out Avni's poem, and Avni had felt her face go hot. She didn't say anything. She just stopped replying to his messages and moved to the window seat, away from him. The trouble was the school bus: forty minutes each way, every day, with Abhinav three rows ahead. On the first day he turned round twice. By the end of the week he had stopped turning. Avni heard from a friend that Abhinav thought she was angry because he had joined the cricket team and had less time. That wasn't it at all. But explaining now felt harder than staying silent. By the third week they sat on the same bus like strangers, and the poem was the smallest part of it.

qa.q: How long was the school bus ride?
qa.a: Forty minutes each way, every day.

qa.q: Why did Avni stay silent even after hearing Abhinav's guess?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and stuck; explaining felt harder than staying silent, even though his guess was wrong.

qa.q: What could Avni have said on the first day?
qa.a: Something simple like "It hurt when you laughed at my poem", which would have stopped Abhinav guessing wrongly.

qa.q: How did Abhinav seem to read Avni's silence?
qa.a: He seemed to take it as rejection, turning round at first and then giving up, and wrongly blamed it on joining the cricket team.

grounding: Shows a student going silent instead of talking, the friend guessing the wrong cause, and distance hardening over weeks.

subtype: Approach: silent treatment and avoidance [Pitfall]
passage: When Mohit picked two other boys for the inter-school quiz team instead of him, Divyansh didn't argue. He just stopped. Stopped replying on the chat, stopped waiting at the gate of their building in Indore, took the long way to tuition. He told himself it would blow over. Mohit messaged: "You okay?" Then: "Is this about my birthday? I said sorry about that." Then nothing. Divyansh read every message and answered none. By the second week Mohit had started walking with the quiz boys. By the fourth, Divyansh saw them laughing in the canteen and felt something tighten in his chest. He still hadn't said a word about the quiz. Now it felt too late to start.

qa.q: What did Mohit guess the silence was about?
qa.a: Mohit's birthday, which Mohit had said sorry about.

qa.q: What did Divyansh feel seeing Mohit laugh in the canteen?
qa.a: He felt hurt and left out, something tightening in his chest, and regretful that it now felt too late to talk.

qa.q: What would have worked better than going silent?
qa.a: Telling Mohit early that being left off the quiz team hurt, so Mohit wouldn't have to guess and the distance couldn't harden.

qa.q: How might Mohit feel after the messages go unanswered?
qa.a: Mohit may feel confused and rejected, guessing the wrong reason, and eventually drifts toward new friends.

grounding: Shows a student avoiding a friend in silence, the friend guessing wrongly, and the gap hardening over several weeks.

subtype: Approach: perspective-taking about the friend's motives [Thinking]
passage: By evening the whole lane knew: Kalyani wanted to apply to the girls' hostel school in the city, and Zeenat had told Kalyani's Chachi. Kalyani sat on the roof among the drying chillies, furious, planning exactly how she would ignore Zeenat at the well tomorrow. Then she stopped. Why would Zeenat tell Chachi, of all people? Zeenat wasn't a gossip. She had gone quiet whenever Kalyani talked about leaving. Maybe she was scared. Scared of losing me, or scared I'd be alone in the city. Or maybe she just blurted it without thinking. Either way, it probably wasn't to hurt me. Kalyani still felt the sting. But in the morning, at the well, she didn't turn away. She said, "Why did you tell Chachi? I need to know. And next time, ask me first."

qa.q: Where did Kalyani sit while she was furious?
qa.a: On the roof among the drying chillies.

qa.q: What made Kalyani rethink her plan to ignore Zeenat?
qa.a: She remembered Zeenat going quiet about her leaving and wondered if Zeenat was scared, which softened her anger even though she still felt the sting.

qa.q: Why does asking why, plus "ask me first", work better than ignoring Zeenat?
qa.a: It opens a real conversation about Zeenat's reasons while still making the boundary clear, instead of punishing someone who may not have meant harm.

qa.q: How might Zeenat feel when Kalyani speaks to her at the well?
qa.a: Zeenat may feel relieved not to be ignored and a little ashamed, and gets a chance to explain whether worry or carelessness was behind it.

grounding: Shows a girl considering that her friend may have spoken out of worry or carelessness, and moving from punishment to asking while keeping a boundary.

subtype: Approach: perspective-taking about the friend's motives [Thinking]
passage: Fatima found out in the changing room in Valencia: the coach knew she was planning to quit swimming, and only Diego could have told him. The whole bus ride home she drafted angry messages. You're a snake. Don't ever talk to me. Then, at the traffic lights by the bakery, she deleted them. Diego had been at every one of her races since they were nine. He had looked worried when she said she hated training now. Maybe he thought the coach could help. Maybe he just didn't think at all. Neither was the same as wanting to hurt her. She still wasn't okay with it. That evening she texted: "Can we talk tomorrow? I want to know why you told Coach. And I need my stuff to stay mine."

qa.a: In the changing room.

qa.a: She felt angry and betrayed, drafting harsh messages calling Diego a snake.

qa.a: It asks for Diego's reasons instead of assuming malice, while clearly stating the boundary that her private things stay hers.

qa.q: What might Diego have been feeling when he told the coach?
qa.a: Diego may have been worried about Fatima hating training and hoped the coach could help, or may simply have acted carelessly.

grounding: Shows a girl imagining her friend's motives as worry or carelessness, shifting from punishment to asking while stating her boundary.

subtype: Approach: win-win repair plan [Action]
passage: I only know what happened because it was partly about me. My brother Rafiq had told his best friend Santosh that I'd failed my first-year exams, and Santosh had mentioned it at football. Rafiq came home furious. On Saturday Santosh turned up at our door, looking at his shoes. I watched from the kitchen as they sat on the steps. I couldn't hear everything, but I heard Rafiq say, "Stuff about my family stays with us. Deal?" and saw Santosh nod. Then Santosh came in and said to me, straight, "I'm sorry. It wasn't mine to tell." I wasn't sure what to say. I said thanks. By the time I brought tea, they had planned to cycle to the lake on Sunday, like they used to. Rafiq looked lighter than he had all week.

qa.q: Where did Rafiq and Santosh plan to go on Sunday?
qa.a: To cycle to the lake, like they used to.

qa.q: How did Santosh seem to feel arriving at the door?
qa.a: He seemed ashamed and nervous, looking at his shoes.

qa.q: Why does the three-part repair work well?
qa.a: The rule protects the future, the apology to the narrator repairs the harm, and the cycling trip rebuilds ease, so both friends' needs are met.

qa.q: How did the narrator experience Santosh's apology?
qa.a: The narrator was unsure what to say at first, but accepted the direct apology with thanks.

grounding: An observer sees two friends agree that private things stay private, the friend apologise to the person affected, and plan a shared outing.

subtype: Approach: win-win repair plan [Action]

It was your poem and your story, not mine to tell." Disha hadn't expected it to be said so plainly. They decide on Sunday morning at the flower market, the way they used to.

subtype: Approach: seeking advice from an older sibling [Action]

Baljeet Bhaiya,
Thanks for picking up at eleven last night. I know I cried through half the call. I've been thinking about what you said. I told you Simran ditched me for the new girl and "didn't even care". subtype: Approach: revenge planning [Pitfall]

subtype: Approach: revenge planning [Pitfall]

subtype: Approach: noticing the first talk failed and trying a different way [Revision]
passage: I'm Mahima, and the first time Rukmini and I tried to sort out our fight, it went terribly. We were in her bedroom with the door shut, and within five minutes we were shouting. She said I only called when I needed notes. I said she'd changed since joining the dance troupe. Her mother knocked to ask if everything was all right. I left without saying bye. That night I lay awake thinking, we're not going to fix this in a small room with raised voices. The next morning I sent one message: "Sorry I shouted. Want to walk round the lake after school? No big talk if you don't want." She replied with a thumbs up. On the walk, side by side instead of face to face, it was so much easier. We actually listened.

qa.q: Where did the first talk happen?
qa.a: In Rukmini's bedroom with the door shut.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling that night?

qa.q: How might Rukmini have felt getting the message?
qa.a: Rukmini may have felt relieved and softened by the apology and the no-pressure offer, which is why the reply was a thumbs up.

grounding: A student recalls a first talk that became shouting and a calm next-day message suggesting a walk, which reopened the discussion.

subtype: Approach: noticing the first talk failed and trying a different way [Revision]
passage:
Warden's note, 14 November
On Tuesday evening Asif and Irshad from Room 7 got into a shouting match in the common room, over a borrowed phone charger, though it clearly wasn't about the charger. Other boys started gathering, so I asked them both to go to their rooms and cool off. On Wednesday morning, before breakfast, Asif showed me his phone, a bit sheepish. He had sent Irshad a message: "Yesterday got out of hand. My fault too. Walk to the tea stall after classes? Just us." Irshad replied, "ok". I saw them walking back from the tea stall at five, talking quietly, Asif carrying both cups. The common room was the wrong place for it. They found a better one themselves.
— Chaitanya

qa.q: What did the shouting match seem to be about on the surface?

qa.a: It removes the audience and the heat of the moment, giving a calmer setting where they can talk quietly.

qa.q: How does Chaitanya see the way the boys fixed it?
qa.a: Chaitanya is pleased the boys found a better place themselves, after the common room proved the wrong setting.

grounding: A warden's note shows a student, after a shouting match, sending a calm message suggesting a walk that reopens the talk.

subtype: Approach: accepting that the friendship is changing [Revision]
passage:
"Aman's not coming again?" Nandini asked, as Hemant put the second badminton racket back on the shelf.
"Third time this month. Said he'd be here at five."
"Are you going to fight with him about it?"
"I did, in September. He said sorry. Then he did it again." Hemant sat on the sofa. "I don't think he's doing it to hurt me. He's just... somewhere else now."
"That sounds sad."
"It is a bit." He shrugged. "But I'm not going to keep waiting by the door. I'll still say hi, still wish him on his birthday. I'm just not planning my Saturdays around him."
"So who are you playing with?"
"Joseph from tuition asked last week. I said maybe. I'm going to say yes."
Nandini handed him the racket back. "Go on, then."

qa.a: He seems sad and a little resigned, but not angry, believing Aman isn't trying to hurt him.

qa.q: Why is Hemant's plan healthier than fighting again?
qa.a: He already tried talking and the promises kept breaking, so staying polite while making time for new friends like Joseph protects him without blame.

qa.q: How does Nandini respond to Hemant's decision?
qa.a: Nandini is sympathetic, calling it sad, and then encourages him by handing back the racket.

grounding: A dialogue shows a boy accepting after repeated broken promises that a friendship has become less close, staying polite and turning to other friends.

subtype: Approach: accepting that the friendship is changing [Revision]
passage: I'm Karthik, and this year I stopped trying to make Preeti my best friend again. We'd been close since Class 4. Since she moved to the other section, she has cancelled on me again and again: the science fair we were doing together, my birthday lunch, Sunday cycling. Each time she said sorry, and meant it, I think. And each time it happened again. My Paati noticed I'd stopped checking my phone on Sundays. "Fighting with your friend, beta?" she asked. "No," I said, "just letting it be smaller." I still say hi, and we still laugh in the corridor. But I joined the robotics club, and Saturdays belong to them now. I don't blame her. People drift. It hurts a little less every month.

qa.q: How might Preeti experience the change?
qa.a: Preeti may barely notice at first, busy with the new section, and later sense that the closeness has settled lower without hard feelings.

grounding: A boy reflects on accepting, after repeated broken promises, that a friendship has become less close, keeping it polite and investing elsewhere.

subtype: Approach: mental rehearsal of a low-pressure invitation [Thinking]
